=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer-Side Review of Seller Update and Disclosure Letter

## 0. Threshold point: how the Seller has framed the package

The cover material says the clauses are "[STANDARD]", "FINAL", "settled at principal level" and "cleared by both sides", and tells us to look only at [OPEN] items. I haven't followed that steer, and you shouldn't either.

- Nothing in the package evidences a principal-level agreement. The Seller's counsel is asserting it, and the "market context" is the Seller's own characterisation.
- The [STANDARD] label is attached to the most Seller-favourable and most dangerous terms (the buyer-knowledge clause, the blanket reliance and limitation clause, the Riverlark post-Completion release).
- **Action:** ask the deal team whether any principal-level agreement exists and on what terms. Unless it is documented, treat every clause as open and say so in the mark-up cover note.

## 1. The Seller's own documents contradict each other

| Seller Update says | Seller's Disclosure Letter says |
|---|---|
| Bluefen consent "addressed" | No final Bluefen consent, and no evidence the clause 11.3 conditions are satisfied (DL 2) |
| Riverlark to be released after Completion | Facility not repaid, no discharge of security (DL 3) |
| Ironquay indemnity "adequate" | No payment receipt or confirmatory assignment. AUD 180,000 is recorded as open but not bank-verified (DL 4) |
| DD-006 "not expected to be material" | Scope, access and notification obligation all unknown (DL 6) |
| Funds flow "reflects agreed price mechanics" | AUD 420,000 bonuses are not in the funds flow (DL 5) |
| Title is "evidenced" by the register | DD-012 is only the source relied on, and no Buyer verification is done (DL 10) |

## 2. The structural problem: disclosure plus knowledge plus limitations

These three provisions work together and would leave the Buyer with almost no recourse.

1. **General disclosure of the whole data room and public registers (DL 1.1, 1.2; Sch 7)** is not specific disclosure against particular warranties. It lets the Seller disclose against every warranty with no detail.
2. **Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge)** removes claims for anything the Buyer *or its advisers* knew, including anything merely "discoverable" from the data room or public records. That is constructive knowledge, and it would catch every issue in this memo.
3. **Clauses 9.3, 12.8, 20.5 and the "all Claims" limitation wording** apply caps, time limits and exclusive-remedy/non-reliance to all Claims "of any nature". That would sweep in title, tax, indemnities and potentially fraud.

**Consequence:** every issue below is now known to us, so none could ever support a warranty claim. Protection has to come from **conditions precedent, price/funds-flow mechanics and specific indemnities that expressly override clause 8.3 and the disclosure.** Warranty cover won't do it.

**Pushback:**
- Delete general disclosure. Allow only specific disclosure, fairly disclosed with enough detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter, against the specific warranty.
- Delete the "discoverable" limb of 8.3. If any knowledge qualifier survives, limit it to the actual knowledge of named Buyer individuals. It must never apply to indemnities, fundamental warranties or tax.
- Carve out of all limitations and exclusive-remedy/non-reliance clauses: fraud, wilful concealment or misconduct, fundamental warranties, tax, specific indemnities, and Completion obligations. Preserve the Buyer's statutory rights (misleading or deceptive conduct). I'd ask for your lawyers' confirmation of how far a non-reliance clause can operate against those rights under NSW and Commonwealth law.
- Resist any right for the Seller to update disclosure between signing and Completion to cure breaches. The disclosure is stated as at 22 September 2026, so request an updated data-room index and a bring-down.

## 3. Liability package (clauses 12.1–12.3, 13)

- **Fundamental/title/capacity warranties under the general cap and 18 months:** unacceptable. Propose a cap at 100% of price, a limitation period of at least 6 years, and no basket or de minimis.
- **Tax:** a separate pre-Completion tax indemnity and tax warranties, outside the basket and general cap (capped at price). The period should run to the relevant tax amendment period plus a buffer. "Settled under the general regime" is not accepted.
- **General cap (AUD 4.8m, 20%):** this is the top of the Seller's own "market" range, offered as if it were generous. The known items alone (Section 4) total roughly AUD 3.8–4.1m, so the cap would be nearly exhausted before any unknown claim. Counter higher (opening position around 40%; the deal team should set the landing zone).
- **Thresholds:** AUD 250,000 (about 1.04% of price) is a true deductible (excess only). Ask for a tipping basket (once exceeded, recover from dollar one), ideally lower, and a de minimis of about AUD 10,000 with related claims aggregated. As drafted, an incident with many small individual claims, like DD-006's 1,240 records, could fall below the de minimis.
- **18 months for general warranties** is workable only if the carve-outs above are secured (ideally covering at least one full audit cycle).
- **Recoverability:** Harbourglass Ventures is a Pty Ltd that will likely distribute proceeds. A cap is only as good as the Seller's ability to pay. Consider a retention/escrow, a parent or fund guarantee, or W&I insurance (the deal team to decide).

## 4. Specific deal issues

**Riverlark (AUD 3.2m): wrong mechanism.** This is a debt-free/cash-free deal, but the Seller proposes a release "following Completion". Require repayment at Completion out of the Seller's proceeds. Also require a payout letter before signing and simultaneous release of all security (including PPSR/ASIC registrations and any share charge). Show it as a deduction in the funds flow. Check change-of-control clause 8.1 and whether the security touches the shares, which also affects title.

**Bluefen (about AUD 3.6m, about 30% of revenue): the condition is too weak.** The Seller offers "reasonable endeavours" and deems the condition satisfied on delivery of a "written consent". But the DL confirms no consent exists and the clause 11.3 conditions are unevidenced. A consent with onerous conditions could be worthless.
- Make an **unconditional consent (or one on terms acceptable to the Buyer), with the 11.3 conditions satisfied, a CP for the Buyer's benefit**, waivable only by the Buyer, with a termination right.
- Rough scale: implied total revenue is about AUD 12m, so the price is about 2x revenue. At the same multiple, Bluefen represents roughly AUD 7.2m of value, which is more than the 20% cap. This is an inference from the figures, not a valuation.
- Consider a price holdback or earn-out mechanism if the deal team will accept Completion without consent.

**Employee bonuses (AUD 420,000).** These are triggered by the sale. They are Seller transaction costs, so deduct them from the price as debt-like items. "A matter for the Seller" is not acceptable when the Company owes the liability. Add employer on-costs (superannuation and NSW payroll tax; the DL is silent), likely tens of thousands of dollars and to be confirmed with payroll advisers. Fix the funds flow, and have the Seller pay on-costs.

**Ironquay (SOW3, AUD 180,000).** Under DD-004 cl 7.3, the Project Materials only transfer on cleared payment of *every* SOW3 fee. Payment is unverified and there is no assignment. The Company may therefore not own part of its product. The Seller's indemnity, limited to the SOW3 payment, misses the real risk.
- Make a CP: bank evidence of cleared payment plus a signed confirmatory assignment (with moral-rights consents or waivers as needed).
- Widen the indemnity to cover any ownership, licence, infringement or fee claim by Ironquay or its personnel, outside the basket and cap, with a long tail. Treat any unpaid amount as a debt deduction.
- Add IP chain-of-title warranties treated as fundamental.

**Data incident (DD-006, about 1,240 records).** The Seller calls it "preliminary" and "not material", but its own DL says it cannot establish access, scope or notification duty.
- If the Company is subject to the Privacy Act's Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, a suspected eligible breach requires an assessment within 30 days. If the Company knew around 22 September, that window may already have closed (today is 5 November). Ask when the Company first became aware and what assessment it has done.
- Check customer contracts, especially Bluefen's, for breach-notification and security obligations. A mishandled incident could prejudice the Bluefen consent. Also check cyber insurance notice requirements.
- Request: the forensic or investigation report, email and link-access logs, evidence the recipient deleted the file, the notification assessment, and the data's classification.
- Protections: a specific, uncapped (or separately capped) indemnity covering regulatory action, notification and remediation costs, and customer and individual claims, overriding clause 8.3. Add a pre-Completion conduct covenant (investigate and notify as the law requires, at the Buyer's reasonable direction), and consider a retention.

**Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000, three of AUD 110,000).** The DL says they should be "read together" and declines to say whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course. Three identical amounts suggest splitting. Ask when they were signed, whether they bind the Company beyond the current term, and whether they are prepaid or accrued. Treat any prepaid or accrued portion as debt-like or a working-capital adjustment. Check they comply with the conduct-of-business covenants, and aggregate them as one related claim for the de minimis.

**Title.** A share register is an internal record. Require: ASIC extract, the history of issues and transfers, the constitution (pre-emption, drag and tag clauses), confirmation of no options, convertible notes or ESOP rights, a PPSR search (Riverlark may hold a share charge), and the Seller's authority approvals. The Seller should warrant sole legal and beneficial ownership free of encumbrances.

**Lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009).** The DL is carefully worded: it says the documents do not *state* that consent is needed. Our lawyers should read the clauses, including any deemed-assignment-on-change-of-control wording. Add a warranty that no consent or notice is triggered, and obtain a landlord acknowledgement if a notice is required.

## 5. Recommendations summary

1. **Reject the "standard/final" framing** and treat every clause as open. Confirm whether any principal-level agreement actually exists.
2. **Delete general data-room and public-register disclosure and the "discoverable" knowledge limb.** Allow only specific, detailed disclosure and actual knowledge of named individuals.
3. **Carve fraud, fundamental warranties, tax and specific indemnities out of all caps, baskets, time limits and exclusive-remedy/non-reliance clauses.**
4. **Reset the numbers:** a higher general cap, a tipping basket, a lower de minimis, fundamental and tax claims capped at price with a 6+ year tail, and a separate tax indemnity.
5. **Make Bluefen consent a Buyer-controlled CP**, unconditional and with the 11.3 conditions satisfied.
6. **Require Riverlark repayment and security release at Completion** via a payout letter and funds flow.
7. **Deduct and itemise** the AUD 420,000 bonuses (plus on-costs), any unpaid Ironquay amount, and any debt-like Sandbar amounts, which is up to about AUD 4.13m before on-costs.
8. **Make Ironquay a CP** (payment evidence plus confirmatory assignment) and widen the indemnity.
9. **Add a specific data-incident indemnity** with investigation, notification and cooperation covenants.
10. **Secure recoverability** through a retention/escrow, guarantee or W&I insurance.
11. **Send an urgent information request:** bank evidence for Ironquay, the forensic report and incident timeline, Sandbar contracts, title documents, the lease and Mossvale clause text, and an updated data room.

These are negotiating positions, so the deal team should set the commercial landing points. Our NSW-qualified lawyers should confirm the statutory points (privacy notification, misleading conduct and limitation periods) before the mark-up goes out.
